name: Kaninuwa
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Park, Joseph & Joyce Park. 2021. Kaninuwa Grammar (version 2021). SIL PNG; also Andersen/Breaden 2001 Kaninuwa OPD (sil.org returns 403; per Glottolog kani1281).

new_statements.quote: Stress is predictable. The penultimate vowel in a word is stressed, with secondary stress on preceding alternate vowels. It is realized as a somewhat lengthened vowel. baguna ‘garden’ [bɑ.ˈɡu.nɑ] fwayafwaya ‘ground’ [ˌfʷɑ.jɑ.ˈfʷɑ.jɑ]
new_statements.citation: Park, Joseph & Joyce W. Park. 2021. Kaninuwa Grammar (version 2021). Ms., 139 pp. Ukarumpa: SIL Language & Culture Archives (item 91825; Glottolog ref 588981).
new_statements.locator: §1.5 Stress, p. 5 (PDF page 11); supporting example §1.3, p. 3 (PDF page 9); fn. 1, p. 2
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable and falls on the penultimate vowel (syllable) of the word; diphthongs (V + higher V within a morpheme, plus /iu/) count as one syllable, so au.na 'his uncle' is [ˈɑu.nɑ] but a.u.na 'I carried' is [ɑ.ˈu.nɑ] (§1.3 p. 3). Stress is cued mainly by slight vowel lengthening.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on preceding alternate vowels, i.e. every second syllable leftward from the penult (fwayafwaya [ˌfʷɑ.jɑ.ˈfʷɑ.jɑ]).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Only caveat: whether a vowel sequence is a diphthong or two syllables changes which vowel is penultimate (§1.3 p. 3).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word ('in a word'); examples are single citation-form words, including a reduplicated form. No statement on phrase-level prominence. Fn. 1 p. 2 says the phonology chapter derives mainly from the Kaninuwa OPD revised in 2006.
new_statements.identity_note: Park & Park 2021 describe Kaninuwa [wat] as spoken in Sivesive (and hamlets) and Kikwanauta on the north coast of Goodenough Island, ~800 speakers — this is Glottolog kani1281 (alt. names Wataluma, Kaokao). Kassell 2012 reports no clear dialect boundaries, so no dialect qualification is needed. Lithgow 1976 refers to the same language as 'Wataluma'.

sources.note: §1.5 Stress, p. 5: stress is predictable, on the penultimate vowel of the word, with secondary stress on preceding alternate vowels, realized as slight lengthening; examples baguna [bɑ.ˈɡu.nɑ], fwayafwaya [ˌfʷɑ.jɑ.ˈfʷɑ.jɑ]. §1.3 p. 3 adds that diphthong vs. two-vowel-sequence analysis affects stress placement (au.na 'his uncle' [ˈɑu.nɑ] vs a.u.na 'I carried' [ɑ.ˈu.nɑ]). Fn. 1 p. 2 says the phonology chapter comes mainly from a Kaninuwa OPD revised in 2006. Obtained from the Wayback Machine snapshot (20240910230728) of the SIL reapdata PDF because sil.org Cloudflare-blocks non-browser fetches.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. Kaninuwa appears as 'Wataluma': p. 170 lists it among languages 'of which nothing is recorded, except survey material'; pp. 455, 460, 468, 478, 517 give location (two villages, north Goodenough), lexicostatistics (51% with Iduna, 44% Bwaidoka, 42% Are) and possessive/subject affix comparisons. Open mirror at sealang.net/archives/pl/pdf/.
